{{Short description|Mathematics formula}}
In [[algebra]], the '''Leibniz formula''', named in honor of [[Gottfried Leibniz]], expresses the [[determinant]] of a [[square matrix]] in terms of permutations of the matrix elements. If <math>A</math> is an <math>n \times n</math> matrix, where <math>a_{ij}</math> is the entry in the <math>i</math>-th row and <math>j</math>-th column of <math>A</math>, the formula is<ref>{{Cite book |last=Strang |first=Gilbert |title=Introduction to linear algebra |date=2016 |publisher=Cambridge press |isbn=978-0-9802327-7-6 |edition=5th |location=Wellesley |publication-date=2016 |pages=260-262}}</ref>
:<math>\det(A) = \sum_{\tau \in S_n} \sgn(\tau) \prod_{i = 1}^n a_{i\tau(i)} = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^n a_{\sigma(i)i}</math>
where <math>\sgn</math> is the [[Even_and_odd_permutations|sign function]] of [[permutation]]s in the [[permutation group]] <math>S_n</math>, which returns <math>+1</math> and <math>-1</math> for [[even and odd permutations]], respectively.

Another common notation used for the formula is in terms of the [[Levi-Civita symbol]] and makes use of the [[Einstein summation notation]], where it becomes
: <math>\det(A) = \epsilon_{i_1\cdots i_n} {a}_{1i_1} \cdots {a}_{ni_n},</math>
which may be more familiar to physicists.

Directly evaluating the Leibniz formula from the definition requires <math>\Omega(n! \cdot n)</math>  operations in general—that is, a number of operations asymptotically proportional to <math>n</math> [[factorial]]—because <math>n!</math> is the number of order-<math>n</math> permutations.  This is impractically difficult for even relatively small <math>n</math>.  Instead, the determinant can be evaluated in <math>O(n^3)</math> operations by forming the [[LU decomposition]] <math>A = LU</math> (typically via [[Gaussian elimination]] or similar methods), in which case <math>\det A = \det L \cdot \det U</math> and the determinants of the triangular matrices <math>L</math> and <math>U</math> are simply the products of their diagonal entries.  (In practical applications of [[numerical linear algebra]], however, explicit computation of the determinant is rarely required.)  See, for example, {{harvtxt|Trefethen|Bau|1997}}. The determinant can also be evaluated in fewer than <math>O(n^3)</math> operations by reducing the problem to [[Matrix multiplication algorithm|matrix multiplication]], but most such algorithms are not practical.

== Formal statement and proof ==

'''Theorem.'''
There exists exactly one function <math> F : M_n (\mathbb K) \rightarrow \mathbb K</math> which is [[Alternatization|alternating]] [[Multilinear_map|multilinear]] with respect to columns and such that <math>F(I) = 1</math>.

'''Proof.'''

'''Uniqueness:''' Let <math>F</math> be such a function, and let <math>A = (a_i^j)_{i = 1, \dots, n}^{j = 1, \dots , n}</math> be an <math>n \times n</math> matrix. Call <math>A^j</math> the <math>j</math>-th column of <math>A</math>, i.e. <math>A^j = (a_i^j)_{i = 1, \dots , n}</math>, so that <math>A = \left(A^1, \dots, A^n\right).</math>

Also, let <math>E^k</math> denote the <math>k</math>-th column vector of the [[identity matrix]].

Now one writes each of the <math>A^j</math>'s in terms of the <math>E^k</math>, i.e.

:<math>A^j = \sum_{k = 1}^n a_k^j E^k</math>.

As <math>F</math> is multilinear, one has

:<math>
\begin{align}
F(A)& = F\left(\sum_{k_1 = 1}^n a_{k_1}^1 E^{k_1}, \dots, \sum_{k_n = 1}^n a_{k_n}^n E^{k_n}\right) = \sum_{k_1, \dots, k_n = 1}^n \left(\prod_{i = 1}^n a_{k_i}^i\right) F\left(E^{k_1}, \dots, E^{k_n}\right).
\end{align}
</math>

From alternation it follows that any term with repeated indices is zero. The sum can therefore be restricted to tuples with non-repeating indices, i.e. permutations:

:<math>F(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \left(\prod_{i = 1}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right) F(E^{\sigma(1)}, \dots , E^{\sigma(n)}).</math>

Because F is alternating, the columns <math>E</math> can be swapped until it becomes the identity.  The [[Even_and_odd_permutations|sign function]] <math>\sgn(\sigma)</math> is defined to count the number of swaps necessary and account for the resulting sign change.  One finally gets:

:<math>
\begin{align}
F(A)& = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \left(\prod_{i = 1}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right) F(I)\\
& = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i
\end{align}
</math>

as <math>F(I)</math> is required to be equal to <math>1</math>.

Therefore no function besides the function defined by the Leibniz Formula can be a multilinear alternating function with <math>F\left(I\right)=1</math>. 

'''Existence:''' We now show that F, where F is the function defined by the Leibniz formula, has these three properties.

[[Multilinear map|Multilinear]]:
:<math>
\begin{align}
F(A^1, \dots, cA^j, \dots) & = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) ca_{\sigma(j)}^j\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\\
& = c \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) a_{\sigma(j)}^j\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\\
&=c F(A^1, \dots, A^j, \dots)\\
\\
F(A^1, \dots, b+A^j, \dots) & = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma)\left(b_{\sigma(j)} + a_{\sigma(j)}^j\right)\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\\
& = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma)
\left( \left(b_{\sigma(j)}\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right) + \left(a_{\sigma(j)}^j\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right)\right)\\
& = \left(\sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) b_{\sigma(j)}\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right) 
  + \left(\sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right)\\
&= F(A^1, \dots, b, \dots) + F(A^1, \dots, A^j, \dots)\\
\\
\end{align}
</math>
[[Alternating map|Alternating]]:
:<math>
\begin{align}
F(\dots, A^{j_1}, \dots, A^{j_2}, \dots)
& = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^n a_{\sigma(i)}^i\right) a_{\sigma(j_1)}^{j_1} a_{\sigma(j_2)}^{j_2}\\
\end{align}
</math>
For any <math>\sigma \in S_n</math> let <math>\sigma'</math> be the [[tuple]] equal to <math>\sigma</math> with the <math>j_1</math> and <math>j_2</math> indices switched.
:<math>
\begin{align}
F(A) & = \sum_{\sigma\in S_{n},\sigma(j_{1})<\sigma(j_{2})}\left[\sgn(\sigma)\left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^na_{\sigma(i)}^{i}\right)a_{\sigma(j_{1})}^{j_{1}}a_{\sigma(j_{2})}^{j_{2}}+\sgn(\sigma')\left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^na_{\sigma'(i)}^{i}\right)a_{\sigma'(j_{1})}^{j_{1}}a_{\sigma'(j_{2})}^{j_{2}}\right]\\
& =\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n},\sigma(j_{1})<\sigma(j_{2})}\left[\sgn(\sigma)\left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^na_{\sigma(i)}^{i}\right)a_{\sigma(j_{1})}^{j_{1}}a_{\sigma(j_{2})}^{j_{2}}-\sgn(\sigma)\left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^na_{\sigma(i)}^{i}\right)a_{\sigma(j_{2})}^{j_{1}}a_{\sigma(j_{1})}^{j_{2}}\right]\\
& =\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n},\sigma(j_{1})<\sigma(j_{2})}\sgn(\sigma)\left(\prod_{i = 1, i \neq j_1, i\neq j_2}^na_{\sigma(i)}^{i}\right)\underbrace{\left(a_{\sigma(j_{1})}^{j_{1}}a_{\sigma(j_{2})}^{j_{2}}-a_{\sigma(j_{1})}^{j_{2}}a_{\sigma(j_{2})}^{j_{_{1}}}\right)}_{=0\text{, if }A^{j_1}=A^{j_2}}\\
\\
\end{align}
</math>
Thus if <math>A^{j_1} = A^{j_2}</math> then <math>F(\dots, A^{j_1}, \dots, A^{j_2}, \dots)=0</math>.

Finally, <math>F(I)=1</math>:
:<math>
\begin{align}
F(I) & = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^n I^i_{\sigma(i)}
= \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{i = 1}^n \operatorname{\delta}_{i,\sigma(i)}\\
& = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \operatorname{\delta}_{\sigma,\operatorname{id}_{\{1\ldots n\}}}
= \sgn(\operatorname{id}_{\{1\ldots n\}})
= 1
\end{align}
</math>

Thus the only alternating multilinear functions with <math>F(I)=1</math> are restricted to the function defined by the Leibniz formula, and it in fact also has these three properties. Hence the determinant can be defined as the only function <math> \det : M_n (\mathbb K) \rightarrow \mathbb K </math> with these three properties.
